headline: Approved September minutes; discussed park master plan ideas, including the historic cemetery, riverfront access, and railroad crossings.
summary: Santa in the Park is set for Saturday, December 5, 2026, from noon to 2:00 p.m., and volunteers and small unwrapped gifts are needed. Public Works buildings on the east side are expected to be removed in about two to three years, during construction of a new garage on the 111-W campus. Members also discussed sewer overflows, bench safety, and a possible memorial policy.
decisions: Approved the September meeting minutes with a date correction.

decision_evidence.quote: The minutes of the September meeting were approved with date correction.

plain_text:
Greeley Park Advisory Committee 
Mines Fall Conference Room 
848 West Hollis Street 
 
 
Date: November 10, 2026 
Call to Order: 5:00 PM by Fran Murphy 
 
Attendees:  
Committee Members: Fran Murphy, Stephanie Ballentine, Vicki Donchess, Kathy Lodi, 
Alyson Galipeau, Kerry Miller, Susan McNamee   
City Planner: Matthew Sullivan 
Alderman: Patricia Klee 
DPW: Director Lisa Fauteux  
Quorum was determined to be present 
Approval of Minutes: The minutes of the September meeting were approved with date correction. 
Santa in the Park 
 Santa in the Park is scheduled for Saturday, December 5, 2026, from noon to 2:00 p.m. Setup 
usually begins around 9:00 a.m. 
 Volunteers are needed. Donated small gifts are welcome and should be delivered unwrapped 
so organizers can sort and wrap them. Public Works also provides additional gifts. Gifts are 
distributed to children from newborns - teenagers.  
 Gift drop-off deadline or location TBD. 
Regular Park Updates on Meeting Agendas 
 Suggestion that DPW or Parks and Recreation share upcoming events and work with the 
Advisory Board - Regular updates could help the group identify opportunities to support park 
projects and events. No formal decision was recorded. 
Greeley Park Map and Items for consideration in a Master Plan led by Matthew 
Sullivan 
 Reviewed a 1907 park plan showing the riverfront, fields, tennis courts, shelters, crossings, 
and proposed roads or entrances. Some roads shown were never built. The map may help 
explain the park’s layout and history.
 The map was due to be returned to the historical society after the meeting on November 10. 
Question was raised re how a copy of the antique map could be made. 
 Discussion of changes to the park’s land area 160 - but its units, context, and the historical 
reason for the changes were unclear. 
 Participants noted prior agreement that the Manchester Street Gateway should remain an 
entrance without becoming a large new public entrance. The current entrance, marked by a 
rope across the drive, may not be recognizable as an entrance. Ideas included a more 
welcoming gateway and a trail-route sign similar to the one at Mine Falls. 
East-Side Area, Historic Cemetery, and Buildings 
 The east side includes the horseshoe pits, park facilities, ball fields, tennis courts, community 
gardens and a historic cemetery. 
 Newspaper research has identified some people buried in the cemetery - gravestones were 
removed and used as fire-pit stones by militia members; exact burial locations are unknown. 
 Question raised of a court order or similar ruling protecting the cemetery area, but the details 
and boundaries are unclear. 
 The current DPW buildings, in much disrepair, are expected to go away for the most part in 
approximately two to three years. During construction of the new garage on the 111-W 
campus. Garage construction is expected to take about two years, and additional equipment 
and staff may be placed in the area during construction. One masonry building may remain. 
  Possible future uses mentioned included expanding the park or community gardens. The 
future use of cleared areas would be up to the Board of Public Works and the Board of 
Aldermen. 
Site Layout, Gardens, Recreation, and Landscape 
 Participants described the east-side area as having developed piecemeal and said a broader 
plan could make its uses and connections clearer. 
 Ideas included expanding the area’s agricultural character. A greenhouse or plant-growing 
program was discussed, but city staff capacity and the lack of a clear operator were concerns. 
 Some participants worried that vehicles and gatherings in a recently cleared area could affect 
the soil if it is later used for gardens. Fencing or other ways to restrict access were discussed, 
but no approach was agreed. 
 Activities in the area include soccer, cricket, softball, horseshoes, and badminton. Soccer was 
described as the most-used activity, and cricket use as growing. A parks representative will 
look into current and historical use of the athletic facilities by towns, groups.
Playground, Bandshell and Park Aesthetics 
 Generally agreed in keeping the playground near the barbecue pits, wading pool, and gazebo.  
 Ideas included moving beyond primary-color plastic equipment, considering wood or more 
intricate designs, and creating features that encourage imaginative play. The existing sensory 
garden was described as overgrown, blocking the view of the Stonehouse. Moving it was 
raised as a possibility. 
 Several participants described the bandshell as unsightly or unfinished in appearance, 
although it was recently updated. A future master plan could reconsider its redesign. 
Riverfront Access, Trails, and Railroad 
 Participants discussed improving access to and enjoyment of the river, including walking and 
hiking routes, trails, seating, picnic areas, an accessible path, fishing, Addition of  picnic tables 
and benches were suggested near the boat ramp. 
 The railroad is active at least twice a day, with cargo trains including coal trains. Access across 
the tracks was identified as a major obstacle, possible upgrade in the crossing? Past efforts to 
work with the railroad owners were unsuccessful, and current contact channels are difficult to 
reach. The NH federal delegation was mentioned as a possible source of support. 
 Concern that increased activity to the waterfront could add traffic on Hills Ferry and affect 
nearby residents.  
Community Events and Attendance 
 The Fairy Tale Festival and Boo Bash were discussed as most popular events, with 
attendance reported at around 4,000. Boo Bash has been more successful since being 
rebranded from Fright Night 
 A city-linked social media page by the Advisory Committee was discussed as a way to share 
information and solicit feedback with the public, but Public Works notes they already have a 
link on the City webpage, and discourages adding to staff workload.
Combined Sewer Overflows and River Water Quality 
 Participants discussed combined sewer overflows (CSOs), their potential effects on the 
Merrimack River and public use. 
 A city representative said the current approach is to focus on areas that still have CSO 
overflows rather than fully separating the sewer system. Full separation was described as 
difficult and costly; stormwater treatment could become a future requirement. 
Benches, Safety, Lighting, and Memorials 
 Participants discussed whether benches could create problems related to people sleeping in 
the park. 
 Parks rep reports the park is closely monitored Security lighting was discussed, particularly 
near the waterfront, buildings, and benches. Participants mentioned finding needles and other 
items in the bathrooms. 
 A policy for park memorials should be considered. 
Future Meetings and Leadership 
 Will use December meeting to recap ideas about park areas already discussed and invite 
additional suggestions. 
 Fran Murphy plans to step down as Chair at the end of this year, and an election of officers in 
December was discussed. 
  
Next Meeting: 5:00 pm, December 9, 2026 
Meeting Adjourned at 6:20pm 
 
Stephanie Ballentine
